{{Short description|Inequality type in mathematical analysis}}
In [[mathematical analysis]], the '''Hardy–Littlewood inequality''', named after [[G. H. Hardy]] and [[John Edensor Littlewood]], states that if <math>f</math> and <math>g</math> are nonnegative [[measurable function|measurable]] [[real functions]] vanishing at [[infinity]] that are defined on <math>n</math>-[[dimension]]al [[Euclidean space]] <math> \mathbb R^n</math>, then

:<math>\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)g(x) \, dx \leq \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f^*(x)g^*(x) \, dx</math>

where  <math>f^*</math> and <math>g^*</math> are the [[symmetric decreasing rearrangement]]s of <math>f</math> and <math>g</math>, respectively.<ref name=liebloss>{{cite book|last1=Lieb|first1=Elliott|authorlink1=Elliott H. Lieb|last2=Loss|first2=Michael|author2-link=Michael Loss|title=Analysis|year=2001|edition=2nd|publisher=[[American Mathematical Society]]|series=Graduate Studies in Mathematics|volume=14|isbn=978-0821827833}}
</ref><ref name=burchard>{{cite book|title=A Short Course on Rearrangement Inequalities|first=Almut|last=Burchard|author-link=Almut Burchard|url=http://www.math.toronto.edu/almut/rearrange.pdf}}</ref>

The decreasing rearrangement <math>f^*</math> of <math>f</math> is defined via the property that for all <math>r >0</math> the two super-level sets 

:<math>E_f(r)=\left\{x\in X: f(x)>r\right\} \quad </math> and <math> \quad E_{f^*}(r)=\left\{x\in X: f^*(x)>r\right\} </math>

have the same volume (<math>n</math>-dimensional [[Lebesgue measure]]) and <math>E_{f^*}(r)</math> is a ball in <math> \mathbb R^n</math> 
centered at <math>x=0</math>, i.e. it has maximal symmetry. 
 
==Proof==
The [[layer cake representation]]<ref name=liebloss/><ref name=burchard/> allows us to write the general functions <math> f</math> and  <math> g</math> in the form 

<math>f(x)= \int_0^\infty \chi_{f(x)>r} \, dr \quad </math>  and <math> \quad g(x)= \int_0^\infty \chi_{g(x)>s} \, ds</math>

where <math> r \mapsto \chi_{f(x)>r}</math> equals <math> 1</math> for <math> r< f(x)</math> and  <math> 0</math> otherwise. 
Analogously, <math> s \mapsto \chi_{g(x)>s}</math> equals <math> 1</math> for <math> s< g(x)</math> and  <math> 0</math> otherwise. 

Now the proof can be obtained by first using [[Fubini's theorem]] to interchange the order of integration. When integrating with respect to <math> x \in \mathbb R^n </math> the conditions <math> f(x)>r</math> and  <math> g(x)>s</math> the indicator functions <math> x \mapsto \chi_{E_f(r)}(x) </math> and <math> x \mapsto \chi_{E_g(s)}(x) </math> appear with the superlevel sets <math> E_f(r)</math> and <math> E_g(s) </math> as introduced above: 

:<math>
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)g(x) \, dx = \displaystyle\int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\int_0^\infty \chi_{f(x)>r} \, dr  \; \int_0^\infty \chi_{g(x)>s}  \, ds \, dx 
= \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \chi_{f(x)>r}\; \chi_{g(x)>s} \, dr \, ds \, dx
</math>
:::<math>= \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\chi_{E_f(r)}(x) \; \chi_{E_g(s)}(x) \, dx \, dr \, ds
   = \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \int_{\mathbb{R}^n}\chi_{E_f(r) \cap E_g(s)}(x)  \, dx \, dr \, ds. </math>

Denoting by <math> \mu </math> the <math> n </math>-dimensional Lebesgue measure we continue by estimating the volume of the intersection by the minimum of the volumes of the two sets. Then, we can use the equality of the volumes of the superlevel sets for the rearrangements:

:::<math>= \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \mu\left(E_f(r)\cap E_g(s)\right) \, dr \, ds</math>
:::<math>\leq \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \min\left\{\mu(E_f(r)),\, \mu(E_g(s)) \right\} \, dr \, ds</math>
:::<math>= \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \min\left\{\mu(E_{f^*}(r)),\, \mu(E_{g^*}(s)) \right\} \, dr \, ds.</math>

Now, we use that the superlevel sets  <math> E_{f^*}(r) </math> and <math> E_{g^*}(s) </math>  are balls in <math> \mathbb R^n</math> 
centered at <math>x=0</math>, which implies that <math> E_{f^*}(r) \, \cap\, E_{g^*}(s) </math> is exactly the smaller one of the two balls:

:::<math>= \int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \mu\left( E_{f^*}(r)  \cap E_{g^*}(s) \right) \, dr \, ds</math>
:::<math>= \int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f^*(x)g^*(x) \, dx </math>

The last identity follows by reversing the initial five steps that even work for general functions. This finishes the proof.
